customerJourneyStories.name: From Informant and spreadsheets to one real estate ERP
customerJourneyStories.summary: The director of a 30-FTE property management and VvE administration firm that has run on Informant since 2004 moves to the platform after the 2025 acquisition: discovering the migration offer through the vendor's letter and a peer, evaluating it on a demo with the firm's own complexes and on the free migration and support-until-2027 terms, running a bounded parallel run on one client portfolio, and renewing on units per FTE.

stages.narrative: The July 2025 announcement that Informant has been acquired lands on the same week as two other signals: the senior administrator who knows every Informant workaround announces retirement, and an institutional client asks for a monthly owner statement and a portal the firm cannot deliver without a weekend of Excel work. The director decides the system, not the people, is the constraint on growth.

The vendor's letter explains the phased migration, that moving to the platform is free of charge and that Informant support continues until 31 December 2027. At a Vastgoedmanagement Nederland meeting the director of a comparable firm describes running letting, technical management, finance and VvE administration in one platform with branded portals, and the reference logos on the vendor site (FIT Vastgoedbeheer, Ruijters, CRMD Vastgoed Management) are firms the director knows.

The vendor demos with two of the firm's own complexes loaded from the Informant export: a rent run, a fault report turned into a work order, a service charge settlement and the resulting owner statement. The director calls two reference customers, asks the controller to check the accounting and bank integrations and the VAT handling, and compares three years of subscription against the cost of the retiring administrator and the Excel hours. Vendor stability under Vortex, the 8.9 support rating and a written migration plan with a parallel run settle the decision.

The trial is a parallel run on one client portfolio of 600 units and four associations: entities, objects, contracts, relations and opening balances are imported, the team runs the next two rent runs and the quarterly VvE contributions in both systems and compares bank reconciliation and owner statements side by side. Two mapping issues in the chart of accounts are fixed within a week and the controller signs off the first period close from the new system.

Within a year every client portfolio and association lives in the platform, the tenant and owner portals carry the firm's brand, the reconciliation and invoice-coding robots run overnight and the weekly management meeting runs from the dashboard. Informant is switched off long before the support deadline and the firm takes on two new mandates without hiring.

Renewal is not a discussion: units per FTE are up, owner statements go out on the third working day, and the implementation consultant has become the director's process adviser. The director joins the customer advisory group, adds the API Platform module for the firm's BI tool, and gives the reference call to the next Informant firm considering the switch.

customerJourneyStories.name: Buying a portfolio and a competitor without buying a back office
customerJourneyStories.summary: The director of a 60-FTE investment and asset management firm already on the platform uses it as the integration engine for growth: triggered by the acquisition of a 2,000-unit residential portfolio and a small regional manager, discovering the migration tooling and the hyper automation add-on through the account manager and a user day, evaluating them on integration time and headcount avoided, piloting on the acquired portfolio, and expanding the subscription as each acquisition is absorbed.

stages.narrative: The fund the firm manages closes on a 2,000-unit residential portfolio held in six entities, and the same quarter the firm agrees to buy a regional property manager with 25 owner clients and its own legacy package. The board asks how both can be absorbed without doubling the finance and letting teams.

The account manager shows how other tenants used the migration tooling to bring acquired portfolios in as new entities, and at the user day a peer investor describes running rent runs, reconciliation and indexation for a 20,000-unit portfolio with robots. The director learns that the hyper automation and API Platform add-ons are switched on per tenant, not re-implemented.

The evaluation is about integration time and headcount: how many weeks to import six entities and 2,000 contracts with opening balances, whether the acquired manager's owners can be moved to the owner portal in a quarter, what the robots remove in reconciliation and invoice coding hours, and what the add-on subscription costs against the three administrators the board expected to hire. A reference call with an investor who did the same decides it.

The acquired portfolio is imported first: entities, objects, units, contracts and relations from the seller's data room, opening balances from the closing statement, bank connections for each entity. The first rent run goes out on time, the reconciliation robot matches most bank lines overnight and the investor dashboard shows the new portfolio next to the old one within six weeks.

The regional manager's clients follow a quarter later through the same tooling; its owners get the owner portal and its tenants the app, its suppliers the supplier portal. The combined firm runs on one platform, one chart of accounts per entity and one management dashboard, and the finance team is the same size as before the two deals.

With the next acquisition already in due diligence, the director treats the platform as part of the buy-and-build plan rather than as an IT cost: the subscription grows with units, the API Platform feeds the fund's BI tool and the director asks the vendor for a German localisation roadmap for the first cross-border portfolio.

customerJourneyStories.name: From calling the office to the tenant app
customerJourneyStories.summary: A family renting from a property manager that has just switched to the platform adopts the branded tenant app: triggered by a failed direct debit and a leak, discovering the app through the manager's letter and the caretaker, evaluating it for trust and simplicity, trying it with one fault report and one payment, and using it for everything since.

stages.narrative: In the same month a direct debit fails after the bank changed the account number, a reminder letter arrives, and the kitchen tap starts leaking. Three phone calls to the manager's office, two of them on hold, leave the family unsure whether the arrears are cleared and when the plumber comes.

The manager's letter about the new system mentions a tenant app in the manager's own name, and the caretaker shows it on his phone during a visit: the invoice, the payment status and a fault report form with photos. The invitation e-mail with the activation link is still in the inbox.

Before activating, the family checks that the app is the one the manager named, that payment goes through iDEAL and that the manager's office sees the same information. The clear split of rent and service charges, the visible direct debit date and the option to add a second account holder win them over.

They report the leaking tap with two photos and pick a morning slot; the plumber's appointment appears the next day and the tap is fixed at the first visit. They update the bank account and pay the open month with iDEAL from the same screen, and the arrears disappear from the overview that afternoon.

The indexation letter and the service charge settlement arrive in the app with the calculation explained; a question on the settlement is answered in the document thread within two days. The app is the first place the family looks when anything about the home comes up.

A year later they add a co-tenant through a change request, download the inspection report to check a scratch on the floor, and rate the handling of a heating ticket five stars. They have not called the office since the tap.

customerJourneyStories.name: A digital move-in from e-signature to deposit refund
customerJourneyStories.summary: A young professional renting a mid-rent apartment from a fund's asset manager experiences the whole tenancy digitally: triggered by a successful application, discovering the portal through the e-signing invitation, evaluating its trustworthiness on the contract and rent-price check, trialling it with the move-in inspection and first payment, living in it for three years and leaving with a same-week deposit refund.

stages.narrative: After weeks of viewings the application for an apartment is accepted; the letting agent explains that the contract will be signed digitally and that everything about the tenancy will run through the owner's tenant portal. The tenant wants to be sure the rent is legal and the deposit is safe before signing.

The e-signing invitation opens the contract, the rent-price check result, the house rules and a portal preview showing the first invoice and the direct debit mandate. The letting agent's e-mail carries the app store links under the asset manager's brand.

The tenant reads the contract clause by clause, checks the indexation clause against the legal cap, sees the rent-price check and the deposit amount confirmed, and looks up the asset manager's reviews. The transparency of the documents and the fact that the deposit confirmation appears in the portal on payment settle the doubt.

The contract is signed on a phone, the deposit and first month are paid with iDEAL, and the move-in inspection is done with the agent on a tablet: photos and meter readings land in the portal the same afternoon, before the keys are handed over.

For three years rent runs by direct debit, the annual indexation letter and settlement appear with explanations, a broken intercom is fixed after a ticket with a photo, and a name change after a marriage is processed through a change request in a week.

Notice is given in the portal, the end date and the inspection appointment are confirmed automatically, the final inspection matches the move-in photos, and the deposit refund arrives the same week with a statement. The tenant asks the next landlord whether they have the same app.

customers.name: Private Property Owner
customers.description: An individual, family or small company that owns rental property or an apartment but does not administer it: a retired couple with six apartments managed by a firm such as FIT Vastgoedbeheer or Ruijters, a dentist whose practice building and two shops are let by a property manager, a family office with a portfolio of forty homes, or the owner of an apartment in a building whose owners' association is administered by a VvE administrator from the Informant base. Wants to know what the property earns, what it costs, what has been paid out and why, wants to approve repairs, quotes and association decisions quickly, and wants every statement, contract, meeting document and tax overview in one place. customerJourneyStories.name: From a quarterly PDF by e-mail to the owner portal
customerJourneyStories.summary: A retired couple owning six apartments managed by a property management firm adopt the firm's owner portal after the firm moves to the platform: triggered by a statement they could not reconcile and a slow repair approval, discovering the portal through the firm's letter and their accountant, evaluating it for accuracy and security, trying it for one quarter, and renewing the mandate on transparency.

stages.narrative: The quarterly statement PDF shows a payout that is lower than expected, with a maintenance line the couple does not remember approving. Two weeks of e-mail with the manager clear it up, but meanwhile a tenant's boiler replacement waits for their approval in an inbox they rarely check.

The manager's letter about the new system announces an owner portal under the firm's name, and the couple's accountant mentions that other clients send him statements straight from such a portal. The manager's account manager offers to activate it and walk through it on a call.

The couple check whether the portal shows exactly the same statement as the PDF, whether every line links to an invoice or bank line, how login and two-factor work, and whether the accountant can be given read access. Seeing the disputed maintenance line with the tenant's fault report, the quote and their own e-mailed approval attached settles their doubts.

For one quarter they use the portal alongside the PDF: the statement appears on the fifth working day with the bank lines behind it, a repair quote arrives as an approval request with photos and is approved from the phone in an hour, and the dashboard shows one apartment with rising arrears before the manager calls about it.

The PDF is switched off. The couple check the dashboard monthly, approve quotes within a day, download the annual statements for the tax return themselves and ask questions in the document thread instead of by e-mail. The accountant works from the portal directly.

When the management agreement comes up for renewal, transparency decides it: the couple renew for five years, move two apartments inherited from a relative to the same manager, and recommend the firm to a friend with a small portfolio.

stages.narrative: The owner misses the annual meeting because the paper invitation arrived while abroad, and learns from a neighbour that the contribution has been raised to fund a roof renovation decided at that meeting. Requests for the minutes and the multi-year maintenance plan take weeks to answer.

The administrator's letter explains that the association's administration is moving from Informant to the platform and that every owner gets a portal with documents, meetings, decisions and the reserve fund. The neighbour who chairs the association shows the agenda for the next meeting already published there.

The owner checks whether the deed of division, house rules, past minutes and the maintenance plan are all there after the migration, whether proxy and online voting are possible, and whether the contribution overview and payment status match the bank statements. The completeness of the migrated history convinces them.

At the next meeting the owner reads the budget proposal in the portal, votes by proxy on the roof renovation contractor, and afterwards sees the recorded decisions, the updated reserve fund statement and the new contribution amount within days.

Contribution invoices, the annual statement, meeting invitations and decisions all arrive in the portal; a leak in the common corridor reported by another owner is followed as a ticket, and the owner approves an extra levy for the lift from a phone while travelling.

When the apartment is sold, the notary's document request is answered with a portal export in a day, and the buyer is invited to the same portal on transfer. The owner asks the administrator of another building they own an apartment in why it does not offer the same.

customers.name: Maintenance Supplier
customers.description: A contractor, installer, plumber, electrician, painter, cleaning company, lift or heating service firm or handyman that does the technical work for organisations on the platform: from a one-person handyman on call for a property manager's residential portfolio to a regional installation company with periodic maintenance contracts for hundreds of boilers, lifts and fire installations. Receives work orders from fault reports and from the periodic maintenance schedule, submits quotes when the work exceeds the mandate, plans visits with tenants, reports completion with photos, updates the installation register and invoices against the work order, either through the branded supplier portal or through a connected partner system such as Ziezodan or Proprli. Uses the portal for free; the organisation pays, and the supplier's self-service is what removes phone calls, disputes and late payments on both sides.
careAbout: Receiving work orders with everything needed to do the job at the first visit: address, access, tenant contact, installation details, photos and the mandate amount
Accepting or declining work in a minute from a phone, and planning visits directly with the tenant instead of through the manager's office
Getting quotes approved quickly so that the job is not lost to waiting
Being paid on time because the invoice matches the work order and needs no chasing
Fewer phone calls and e-mails per job, and one place where all jobs for all clients on the platform are visible
Being a preferred supplier because completion reports, ratings and response times show the quality of the work
winsThem: A supplier portal that shows every open work order across all the organisations that use the platform, with accept, quote, plan, complete and invoice actions
Tenant availability and contact details on the work order, and appointment confirmation sent to the tenant automatically
Automatic reminders from the installation register for periodic maintenance, so the annual boiler or lift visits are planned without a call
Invoice submission against the work order with automatic matching and a visible payment status, or through the partner integration the supplier already uses
Completion reports with photos that close the ticket for the tenant and the owner at the same time
theirFear: Driving to a job where nobody is home, the key is not there or the installation details are wrong, and not being paid for the wasted visit
An invoice that sits in an inbox for months because it does not match a purchase order nobody sent
Losing a good client because a competitor is easier to work with digitally

customerJourneyStories.name: From phone calls and PDF invoices to the supplier portal
customerJourneyStories.summary: A five-person plumbing and heating company working for two property managers adopts the supplier portal when one manager moves to the platform: triggered by wasted visits and a late invoice, discovering the portal through the manager's invitation, evaluating it for effort and payment reliability, trying it on a week of jobs, and asking its other clients for the same.

stages.narrative: In one week a technician drives to an apartment where the tenant is not home because the appointment was passed on by phone through the manager's office, a job turns out to need a boiler part nobody mentioned, and an invoice from three months ago is still unpaid because it cannot be matched to an order. The owner of the company spends Friday afternoon on the phone.

The property manager's technical manager sends an invitation to the supplier portal in the manager's brand and explains that from now on jobs, quotes, appointments and invoices run through it. A colleague installer who already works for a platform organisation shows the app on his phone with the day's jobs and tenant contacts.

The owner checks how much extra work the portal means per job, whether the own planning software can be connected through the Ziezodan integration, whether the tenant's availability and access details are really on the order, and whether invoice status is visible. The promise that a matched invoice is paid within the agreed term without chasing decides it.

The first week's jobs arrive with photos, tenant slots and the mandate amount; technicians accept from the phone, appointments are confirmed to tenants automatically and every job is fixed at the first visit. A quote for a boiler replacement is approved by the owner in a day, and the first invoice submitted against a work order shows as approved for payment within 48 hours.

All jobs for the manager run through the portal or the connected planning system, periodic boiler maintenance orders arrive from the installation register each autumn, completion reports with photos close tickets without a call, and the company's first-time-fix rate and response time appear on its supplier profile.

The company becomes preferred supplier for the manager's residential portfolio and asks its second property manager client, still on Informant, whether they will offer the same portal after migration. Late invoices have disappeared from the Friday afternoon.

customerJourneyStories.name: An installation company onboarded through the installation register
customerJourneyStories.summary: A regional installation company with maintenance contracts for lifts, fire installations and heating in an investor's commercial portfolio adopts the platform's periodic maintenance flow: triggered by a missed inspection and a compliance question from the investor, discovering the installation register through the technical manager, evaluating it on data quality and integration, trialling it on one building's installations, and staying because the register and the invoices now run themselves.

stages.narrative: An annual fire installation inspection in an office building is missed because the reminder lived in a spreadsheet on a departed employee's laptop; the investor's asset manager asks for proof of compliance across the portfolio and the installation company cannot produce it without a week of searching.

The investor's technical manager explains that every installation is now in the platform's register with next inspection dates and that maintenance orders and reminders are generated from it and sent to the supplier portal or through the Proprli integration. The installation company sees its contracted installations listed with certificates and service history.

The company checks whether the register data matches its own records, whether certificates and inspection reports can be uploaded per installation, whether scheduled orders can be planned in bulk per building and whether its service management system can connect. A joint clean-up of the register for one building shows the data can be trusted.

For one building the annual lift, fire and heating inspections are executed from generated maintenance orders, planned in bulk, reported with certificates uploaded per installation, and invoiced against the orders; the investor's compliance overview turns green for that building without an e-mail.

The whole contracted portfolio moves to the register-driven flow: reminders arrive weeks ahead, replaced installations are registered with serial numbers by the technician on site, and the investor's asset manager pulls the compliance report for lenders from the platform.

At contract renewal the installation company's on-time inspection rate and complete certificate coverage are the argument for a three-year extension, and it proposes the same register-driven flow to its other clients on the platform.
